speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Good day.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In the meeting just concluded, the FOMC decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by a ¼ percentage point to 3¾ to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: As noted in the policy statement, released just a short while ago, economic activity is expanding at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: While uncertainty remains elevated—owing, in part, to geopolitical developments—domestic spending has been resilient.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Productivity growth—strong; and capital investment is robust.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But inflation remains elevated.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This Committee will deliver price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Now I’ll get into some further detail.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Our decision comes at a time when the American economy appears to be strengthening.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: New hiring, private-sector earnings, business capital investment—each of these markers has improved in recent months and is pointing in a good direction.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Credit flows have been robust, particularly for businesses.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And, as I said at the policy symposium in Jackson Hole, I would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This view was widely shared by the Committee.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So we removed a dose of accommodation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Consider the geopolitical landscape of shocks and uncertainty, and you begin to appreciate the resilience of the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Given that resilience, and the potential for even greater performance, an attitude of optimism is exactly what I heard inside the FOMC these last two days.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: One basic sign of strength is the state of America’s labor markets.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The jobless—the jobless rate remains low at around 4.1 percent, and both job openings and weekly hours have been increasing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Unemployment claims, on a four-week moving average, are running at levels consistent with full employment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So the labor side of the Fed’s congressional remit is in good shape.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yet, for more than five years, inflation has been running above target.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So our predominant focus is on the price-stability side of our mandate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Based on the most recent CPI and PPI data, the 12-month change in total PCE prices likely was around 3.6 percent in August.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Core PCE and CPI prices are running at about 3.2 and 2.4 percent, respectively.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Too many categories are still posting increases above 3 percent on both a 6- and 12-month basis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I noted in Jackson Hole that overall commodity prices also bear watching.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And, over the intermeeting period, the prices of many of these key inputs have risen.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Since my first FOMC meeting as Chairman in June, my colleagues and I have been unequivocal in our commitment to price stability and to our 2 percent PCE inflation objective.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: At our July meeting, we all agreed that inflation remained too high, and we expressed our joint readiness to act as circumstances might require.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And a good majority of my colleagues and I thought the wiser course then would be to await new information in the intermeeting period.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Last month in Wyoming, I expressed my commitment to a monetary policy discipline, not to a decision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I defined the standard for action.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Today the FOMC decided that this standard has not been satisfied.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The Committee’s unanimous vote shows our resolve to achieve price stability on a timelier basis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We aim to ensure that credit and financial conditions are consistent over time with our mandate, that relative price changes in some sectors of the economy do not broaden, that inflation compensation in market prices stays low, and that inflation expectations remain well anchored.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This afternoon, you also received the Summary of Economic Projections.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It reflects the views of my colleagues on the Committee, but, as in June, I have not offered a projection of my own.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But, like in June, I said I would faithfully discharge the summary of their projections, so here goes.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In the summary’s median projections, real GDP rises at 2.3 percent this year, 2.4 percent next year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Total PCE inflation runs at 3.7 percent this year and falls to 2.3 percent next year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The unemployment rate holds steady at about 4.1 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The median participant judges that the appropriate federal funds rate to be 4.1 percent at the end of this year and to remain there next year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Inflation risks are to the upside while labor risks are roughly balanced.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In my meetings these last few weeks—in Jackson Hole; in Asheville at the G-20 meeting, which the U.S. hosted; and at a central bank conference in Basel—it was evident that most advanced economies are facing price pressures.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Their central banks are making their own judgments, consistent with their own remits.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Our decision today reflects our best judgment in service to our remit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The Fed has a role in sustaining the economic progress happening in America right now and the rising opportunities that come with it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Those who are least well off have the most to gain from a durable expansion, a solid labor market, and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We at the Fed are unwavering in our vital and straightforward purpose: full employment and price stability, and a thriving American economy that sets the standard for the world.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And, with that, I’ll take a few of your questions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s a—it’s a—it’s a good question, Richard.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We cannot affect any individual price, whether it be oil prices, whether it be foodstuffs at the grocery store.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But what we can do, and will do, is ensure that any change in relative prices don’t broaden out, don’t have second- and third-order effects in the economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s what we’re tasked to do, and that’s what we will do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So we’re trying to get to more people, so now I get to cherry-pick my preferred question from you, Colby.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This won’t surprise you: I’m not in the forward guidance business.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The decision we made today was a sober decision, serious decision, responsible decision, one that we have been preparing for and thinking about in my 110 or 20 days here.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You heard from other people in the dots effectively, what their forecasts are.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m not going to prejudge any future decisions we make.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You might have heard me say in Jackson Hole, I committed to a discipline, a set of principles.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I committed to look outside the window and see what I can observe.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s what I did in Jackson.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s what we did today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I’ve said this before—I’ll repeat it: The Fed has an enormous amount of power.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: These are decisions we make.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But getting the understanding right between financial markets and the Fed is a balance that I’ve long thought could be better struck.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation, based on our assessment of the trajectory for employment, based on our judgment on the strength of the economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Sometimes the market tries to prejudge our outcomes.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll observe market prices and, and see what they have to say.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But today was our decision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve got nothing for you on the—on the discussion with the President.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So—but I won’t make that count as your question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: On the American people, as I said in my prepared remarks, the least well off are the ones who have the most to gain from stable prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The decision we made today was the right decision to deliver on the remit that Congress gave us to ensure stable prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Moreover, I would say, because of the underlying strength of the economy, because we are, as I mentioned, largely acting consistent with full employment, we can be focused on stable prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Some months ago, I said we will deliver stable prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Today’s action is consistent with that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So, as you might know, I’m not a data-point-dependent guy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I won’t—I won’t react one way or another to data that, that shows up on our doorstep.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: First, I would say a good majority of my colleagues seven weeks ago thought seven weeks is a good investment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s a way to buy time so we could make a wise decision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll highlight three things that have happened in that intermeeting period.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: One is, I made out a judgment seven weeks ago about the strength of the economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There’s been a pretty wide-ranging set of data, including in the labor markets, that the economy has strengthened.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You might have heard me say that in Jackson Hole a few weeks ago.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s a judgment that I have, and the Committee has.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Second, inflation trends—I said in Jackson Hole, trends matter.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I said in Jackson Hole, we need to look outside the window and interrogate reality.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My judgment some weeks ago was, the inflation summer trends weren’t passing the test.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve seen very little information since that would make me reverse that decision, so I’ve stuck with it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And the third thing that’s changed in seven weeks is geopolitics.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And there’s no hiding from hot spots around the world, and our judgment about what is the most likely, or least likely, of the geopolitical situation has changed.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: All three of those things led—lend themselves to a firm, unanimous decision today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve described previously I found it difficult to describe financial conditions as restrictive.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think I said I was hard pressed.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I heard around the table in the last couple of days is, my colleagues were hard pressed to describe it that way, too.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We removed a dose of accommodation so that financial and credit conditions would be more consistent with our ultimate objectives.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That was the decision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That was our judgment, and we’ll continue to evaluate that prospectively.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In a word, no.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In a few words, I’d say this.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve always been interested in a neutral rate as an academic matter.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Back when I learned economics, we used to think of it as a Wicksellian rate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s a real equilibrium rate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s useful academically.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s, it’s a discussion to help us think about policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: No, I don’t.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So market participants and reporters, I think generally over the course of the last decade or so, have grown accustomed to waiting somewhat breathlessly on a data point.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That isn’t my view.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I was not waiting breathlessly on what any particular data was, whether it was retail sales this morning or a CPI “print” last week.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll just reiterate: Trends matter.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Data points are noisy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Data point dependence is a dangerous preoccupation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s not something that concerns me.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Markets over time will come to understand how this Fed makes its decisions, what’s relevant and not, and I wouldn’t want to editorialize that for them beyond it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s a fair question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In the macroeconomics, we tend to look at aggregates around here, aggregate GDP, overall labor market trends, the state of inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: A lot of people in Washington spend a lot of time on distributional consequences, and that’s their job and their business.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I was referring to in the least well off tend to be people that don’t own financial assets—call that a bit less than 50 percent of the country.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They don’t have equity in their home.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They don’t have equity in a 401k plan.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So they’re living off their paycheck that comes every couple of weeks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The thing that we can do consistent with our mandate is two things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And we’ve done that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That doesn’t mean that individuals aren’t searching for a job, but in aggregate, we’re running more or less at full employment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If so, we can then look at the other side of the—our mandate, and let that be our focus.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And stable prices, an environment where inflation is running consistent with our 2 percent objective, offers good news.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Because that way, when they get their wages, they can put their head above water and deliver real take-home pay increases.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We don’t have total responsibility for it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But we do have responsibility for stable prices—as I’ve said before, inflation is a, is a choice—and today we took a step in delivering it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Well, I don’t ask them to prejudge decisions that we’re going to make, so I won’t prejudge decisions that they make.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I will say this, I’ve spent some time with foreign central bank counterparts, not just in the last 20 years, but over the course of the last several weeks, as I mentioned, in Jackson Hole, at the G-20 meeting we hosted in North Carolina, and at a central bank meeting in Basel.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I heard around the table from most of the advanced economies is they’re suffering from price pressures, too.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And they’re making their own choices consistent with their remit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It tells me a couple things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: One is, when the Federal Reserve makes a policy choice, it matters not just to the U.S. economy, but it spills over to the rest of the world.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: To a lesser extent, that’s true for them, too.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: When foreign central banks make decisions, where they’re confronted with higher prices, and they choose, consistent with their remit, to raise rates, then they’re helping to quash inflation in their countries.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And there’s spillovers and spillbacks in both directions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Beyond that, I won’t opine on what other central banks may choose to do this week or beyond.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I don’t—I don’t remember the full context, but I can tell you, Nick, about the state of growth now.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My suspicion, 110 or 20 days ago when I showed up, was that the U.S. economy was strengthening.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Even over the last several weeks I think we now have data broadly defined that says the economy has indeed strengthened.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Underlying growth is higher.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Inflation is the problem.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Stable prices have been the problem for now more than five and a half years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So what the Committee decided to do today was take an action to ensure a timelier return to our price-stability objective.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Price stability is foundational to economic growth, and I think we took an important step today to deliver it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And we did it in part by removing the dose of accommodation that I—that I mentioned before.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Let me speak to the history.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What bond market prices do prospectively, I want to let them do—I want to let them tell me any story they wish to.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I want to try to interrogate that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll give you three, three reasons, but I would say these things tend to be overdetermined.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This is a complicated set of things that are affecting the most important asset anywhere in the world, the 10-year Treasury.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s the risk-free asset upon which every price of virtually every asset in the world is related to.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I’ll say three things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: First is economic strength.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Part of the reason why we’ve seen, over the course of 2026, long-term yields go up is, the economy has strengthened.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Second reason, competition for capital.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The surge in capital expenditures, which I referenced in my remarks, is real, and the so-called hyperscalers are out in the market raising funding.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And so the competition for capital is real, and I think it partly explains the increase in yields.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The third is geopolitics.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The situation hot spots around the world are driving long-term yields.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s not simply spot prices of energy or spot prices for corn or soybeans or wheat, but it’s the difference between those spot prices and so-called crack spreads—what that means for products that find their way into stores across the country.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think those are the three leading explanations but certainly not an exclusive list.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: One easy way to square that, Mike, is those aren’t my forecasts.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Those are the forecasts of my 18 colleagues, and I’ve tried to represent them dutifully to you.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My business is to not give forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But my commitment in June was to reaffirm to the American people, to anyone listening, that we will deliver price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My commitment in July was to say, we want to buy a little bit of time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We want to evaluate what’s happening across a range of dimensions, and what I said in Jackson Hole in August is, we’re committed to a discipline, not to a decision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Today’s action starts to show we’re serious about this.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And we will deliver on the price-stability objective, and as the statement said, we’ll do it on a—on a timelier basis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s our decision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And when we continue our discussions over the course of the next several weeks and months, we’ll have more to say about it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I’m ill-prepared to prejudge those future actions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about AI, and before I found my way to this post, I spent a lot of time talking about it publicly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Independence of the Federal Reserve is about staying in our lane.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We care very much about what’s happening in artificial intelligence.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We care much about the implications on the demand side of the economy and ultimately on the supply side of the economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I care so much—I think it’s so important—that we established a task force that should report by the end of the year to help us think about the implications for our future policy conjuncture.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But the policy decisions that are made about the risks and rewards, the challenges and opportunities, those are decisions made by other parts of the government.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m going to leave it to them to make those political decisions, those policy decisions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The implications of those decisions obviously have some bearing on our day job, and that’s where we’ll be focused.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So, there’s, there’s, there’s a lot there, Jennifer.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Let me see if I can’t do just a little bit of it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: First, we believe that the unemployment rate is basically running consistent with full employment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t believe that we need to do harm to the labor markets to achieve our objective.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t believe that the two parts of our mandate, price stability and full employment, are working at cross purposes over the medium term.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So economic growth—that is ensuring continuous, sustainable, durable, economic growth—that’s the business we’re in.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And the job we did today, the job we’ll continue to do, is to ensure price stability, which can mean that sustainable, durable, economic growth can go on for longer.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The economy can be stronger, and as I mentioned before, the least well off can get the benefits of it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Thank you.
